extra.message: Pickle deserialization of fully user-controlled input via POST body and query params. An attacker can craft a malicious pickle payload that executes arbitrary code upon unserialization at runtime. This is remote code execution.

User-supplied 'host' query parameter is directly concatenated into an os.system() shell command without any sanitization. An attacker can inject arbitrary system commands via delimiter characters (e.g., '; rm -rf /').

User-supplied 'lane' query parameter flows directly into RedirectResponse with no validation. An attacker can craft a URL like /ops/after/loan-return-lane-009?lane=https://evil.com to phish credentials or spread malware.

User-supplied 'card' query parameter is passed through Jinja2 Template.render() and rendered as HTMLResponse. The |safe filter in the template defeats auto-escaping, allowing reflected XSS via crafted URLs.

User-supplied 'fragment' query parameter is concatenated directly into a Jinja2 template string. Attackers can supply template payloads like {{ config }} or {{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }} to read config, exfiltrate secrets, or achieve RCE.

SSL certificate verification is disabled via ssl._create_unverified_context(), and the request goes to 'https://partner.invalid/status'. This pattern enables SSRF against internal services that would normally be unreachable, with no input validation and MITM protection bypassed.

User-supplied 'ref' query parameter (or JSON payload field) is used directly in a file path without sanitization. An attacker can provide '../etc/passwd' as ref to write files outside the intended directory, effectively achieving arbitrary file write.

User-supplied 'name' parameter (defaults to query param) is used directly as filename in target = BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name with no path traversal protection or extension validation. An attacker can write arbitrary files outside the intended directory.

Session cookie is set with secure=False (line 49-57), meaning session tokens will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections. This exposes session credentials to network interception on any non-TLS connection.

cwe: CWE-614: Sensitive Cookie in 'Secure' Field Without Proper Validation

extra.message: Default database connection string contains hardcoded credentials (lending_user:lending_pass) and the secret_key has a clearly marked dev password. These defaults are shipped with the application and could be exploited if never changed in staging or production environments.

When debug=True, the Swagger UI (docs) and OpenAPI schema are exposed at /api/docs and /api/openapi.json. If an operator sets debug=True in production (which is common for troubleshooting), all API endpoint definitions become publicly accessible, potentially leaking sensitive schema information.

ssl._create_unverified_context() explicitly disables TLS/SSL certificate verification on all outbound HTTPS requests. An active network attacker can perform man-in-the-middle attacks to intercept or modify data transmitted to the partner service.

The endpoint at loan-vault-stash-235 returns data containing hardcoded SSN (111-22-3333) and payment card number (4111111111111111) as default values. This is a test/demo code pattern that exposes sensitive financial identifiers in both the file content and API responses.

DEMO_PASSWORD is hardcoded as a plaintext string in the seed file. While primarily used for seeding demo accounts, this constant is printed to stdout in cleartext (line 481) and could leak via logs when operators run the seed script.

Seed script prints all demo account credentials (password and admin API key) in cleartext to stdout. While useful during local development, this creates credential leakage in CI logs, container logs, or any environment where stdout is captured.
